claims.text: A tailored thermomechanical treatment can invert the microstructure of a Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The conventionally processed Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20-based alloy has a continuous ordered B2 matrix containing discrete BCC precipitates.
Controlled hot isostatic pressing at optimized pressure and temperature can trigger the proposed phase-topology inversion.
The resulting inverted microstructure will consist of a continuous ductile BCC matrix with finely dispersed discrete B2 precipitates.
A continuous disordered BCC matrix permits greater dislocation mobility and therefore improves ductility relative to a continuous ordered B2 matrix.
Discrete B2 precipitates impede dislocation motion and provide precipitation strengthening.
Making B2 discrete rather than continuous avoids the brittleness associated with a continuous ordered B2 phase.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than the continuous-B2 baseline at 1023–1123 K.
The treated alloy will have greater ductility than the continuous-B2 baseline at 1023–1123 K.
Conventionally processed refractory high-entropy alloys with a continuous B2 matrix typically have high yield strength.
Conventionally processed refractory high-entropy alloys with a continuous B2 matrix typically have limited ductility at elevated temperature.
The proposed strength and ductility improvements should hold over 1023–1123 K.
Testing at unspecified service-relevant strain rates over 1023–1123 K simulates the intended extreme-environment applications.
The effect may change for different refractory-alloy chemistries or outside 1023–1123 K.
Prior evidence shows that phase-topology inversion can improve room-temperature compressive ductility while retaining high yield strength at room and elevated temperature.
Long-term stability of the inverted microstructure under cyclic high-temperature exposure is unverified.
